newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM DENIES STRIKING DEALS WITH MEDIA BARONS
The Prime Minister has denied he's struck a deal with Rupert Murdoch which would allow him to increase his stake in Channel Seven in exchange for support for Kerry Packer's Fairfax takeover bid.
This follows speculation that a deal had been done over media laws, prompting an angry response from Channel Seven Chairman, Kerry Stokes, who described it as "discraceful".
Mr Howard says there was no deal.
HOWARD CONGRATULATES NEW BRITISH PM
Prime Minister, John Howard has offered his congratulations to new British Prime Minister, Tony Blair.
Mr Howard says it was an outstanding victory.
He's also sent commiserations to defeated Conservative Prime Minister, John Major.
Mr Howard says Mr Major is a good friend who fought a courageous personal campaign in quite impossible circumstances.
WOOLDRIDGE SAYS AUSTRALIA CAN LEARN FROM NZ ON HEALTH
The Federal Health Minister says Australia can learn from New Zealand's success in improving indigenous health.
Michael Wooldridge has told a meeting of obstetricians and gynaecologists in Brisbane, Australia is only now addressing the problems with indigenous health that New Zealand dealt with 40 years ago.
Doctor Wooldridge says in the last 40 years the mortality rate of Maori people has been reduced from 18 years less than the expectancy of non-indigenous people, to between three and four years.
He says in international terms that's an extraordinary achievement.
Dr Wooldridge says Australia can learn from New Zealand by returning the responsibility of indigenous health to Aboriginies.
MCDONALD SAYS MORE LIBS WANT EXTINGUISHMENT
The Federal President of the National Party says there's growing support in the Liberal Party for the blanket extinguishment of native title on pastoral leases.
Don McDonald says the Prime Minister's 10-point plan on native title is too complicated and is open to legal challenge.
He says members of the Liberal backbench are coming to realise the plan fails to offer certainty to anyone involved in the native title debate.
AIDWATCH RESPONDS TO AID REVIEW
The Federal Government's review of Australia's overseas aid program has been criticised for ignoring the needs of the people in recipient countries.
The review, chaired by businessman Paul Simons, urges the Government to reduce the number of countries it gives money to, and to ensure the aid program is focussed primarily on poverty alleviation.
The review also recommends the United Nations aid spending target of at least point-seven per-cent of GDP be abandoned.
The group AIDWATCH says while the review talks about poverty alleviation, the real needs of people in third world countries were not properly considered.

AIDWATCH says an effective and equitable aid program can only succeed if it reflects the needs of local people as they express them, not seen as from a distant Government, whether their own or Australia's.
Meanwhile, the Opposition's Foreign Affairs spokesman, Laurie Brereton, has expressed concern about the review's recommendation that the number of countries receiving Australian aid be cut.
Mr Brereton says this may provide convenient cover for the fiscal neanderthals in the Howard Government to further reduce overseas aid in this month's budget.
He says further cuts to the aid budget will be contrary to the national interest.
CALL FOR REVIEW OF MOBILE PHONE SAFETY STANDARDS
The Australian Democrats have written to Federal Communications Minister, Richard Alston, calling for a review of mobile phone safety standards.
Democrats Telecommunications spokesperson, Lyn Allison, says despite recent evidence mobile phones may increase cancer risks, there is little questioning of whether the standard itself is safe.
Senator Allison says it's not clear who has responsiblity for standards and she wants a review.
She also says it's worthwhile examining the regulatory structure and the capability of the Telcommunications regulator, Austel, to properly monitor mobile phone emissions.
DOWNER SAYS NEIGHBOURS NOT CONFUSED OVER GOVT STAND
The Foreign Affairs Minister says confused signals are not being sent to Australia's regional neighbours.
Alexander Downer's warned Ms Hanson's criticism of Australia's immigration policies and spending on Aboriginal people could cripple our economic and political relations.
But he believes Asian Governments are well aware of the Government's opposition to the views of Pauline Hanson.
On another matter, Mr Downer says Australia's overseas aid dollars need to be seen to being effectively spent if the aid program is to maintain public support.

He's received an independent review of Australia's aid program that recommends the UN aid spending target be abandoned. Mr Downer says he believes the Australian public wants to see aid spending focus on alleviating poverty.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
